name: Senso-ji
why: Tokyo's oldest temple, with the Kaminarimon gate and the Nakamise shopping street. The main hall dates from the 1950s rebuild.
best: Go at sunrise or after dark. The crowds are much smaller then, and the lit hall looks calm.
booking: Entry is free. You do not need a ticket.

name: Meiji Jingu
why: Forest shrine in Shibuya dedicated to Emperor Meiji. A wide gravel path through the trees leads to the main hall.
architect: Ito Chuta led the construction, 1915 to 1920; rebuilt 1958
best: Go in the morning for quiet paths. The Inner Garden shows fall color in late November.
booking: Entry to the shrine is free. The Inner Garden asks for a 500 yen donation.

name: Tokyo National Museum
yomi: とうきょうこくりつはくぶつかん
why: Largest collection of Japanese art and artifacts. The 1938 Honkan building holds the main Japanese galleries.
best: Go on a weekday morning and allow about three hours. Combine it with a walk through Ueno Park.
booking: Buy tickets online to skip the gate line. They cost 1,000 yen and stay valid for two months. The museum closes on Mondays.

name: Mori Art Museum
why: Contemporary art museum on the top floors of the Mori Tower in Roppongi Hills.
best: Go on a clear evening. The museum stays open until 10 pm on most days, and the city lights look best after dark.
booking: Buy tickets online for your chosen exhibition. The museum closes at 5 pm on Tuesdays.

name: teamLab Borderless (Azabudai Hills)
kanji: チームラボボーダレス
yomi: チームラボボーダレス
why: Immersive digital art museum in Azabudai Hills. It reopened here on February 9, 2024, after leaving Odaiba.
architect: Heatherwick Studio and Pelli Clarke Pelli (Azabudai Hills), 2023
best: Go on a weekday for shorter lines. Allow two to three hours inside.
booking: Buy timed tickets online in advance. Closed days vary, so check the calendar before you book.

name: Nezu Museum
why: Kengo Kuma building with Japanese and East Asian art. A large stroll garden with a pond lies behind it.
best: Go on a weekday morning. The garden colors peak from late November to early December.
booking: Buy timed tickets online. Same-day tickets at the door are not guaranteed. The museum closes on Mondays.

name: Tokyo Station
why: Red-brick station that opened in 1914. A 2012 restoration rebuilt its two domes.
best: Visit at dusk, when the Marunouchi facade glows in the evening light.
booking: Viewing the building is free. A room at the Tokyo Station Hotel needs an advance booking.

name: Yoyogi National Gymnasium
yomi: こくりつよよぎきょうぎじょう
why: Kenzo Tange's 1964 Olympic arena with a suspension roof. It became an Important Cultural Property in 2021.
best: View the outside in daylight. Soft morning light shows the curved roof well.
booking: Viewing the outside is free. The inside opens only for events, so check the event calendar.

name: Akihabara Electric Town
yomi: あきはばらでんきがい
why: Shops for electronics, anime, games, and manga. It is the center of Japanese pop tech culture.
best: Go in the afternoon or early evening, when the shops are open and the neon signs light up.
booking: You do not need tickets. Many shops accept credit cards.

name: Miraikan (National Museum of Emerging Science and Innovation)
yomi: にほんかがくみらいかん
why: Science museum in Odaiba with robotics, space, and future-tech exhibits. It opened in 2001.
best: Go on a weekday morning, then enjoy the Tokyo Bay views from Odaiba at sunset.
booking: Buy tickets online up to one week ahead. Adult entry costs 630 yen. The museum closes on Tuesdays.

name: Shinjuku Gyoen
why: Large garden that mixes Japanese, French, and English styles. Chrysanthemum shows run in the first half of November.
best: Go on a weekday morning. Chrysanthemums bloom in early November, and tree colors build toward late November.
booking: Entry costs 500 yen and needs no booking. The garden closes on Mondays, except during the chrysanthemum season.

name: Nezu Shrine
why: Quiet shrine whose main buildings date from 1706 and count as Important Cultural Properties. A path of red torii climbs the hillside.
best: Go on a weekday morning for quiet. The azalea festival in spring is the busy season, so fall is calm.
booking: Entry is free. You do not need a ticket.

name: Omotesando Hills
yomi: おもてさんどうヒルズ
why: Tadao Ando's shopping complex from 2006 on Omotesando. A long sloping ramp winds through its atrium.
best: Visit on a weekday morning, when the ramp is quiet.
booking: Entry is free. You do not need a ticket.

name: Dior Omotesando
yomi: ディオールおもてさんどう
why: Glass building by SANAA (Sejima and Nishizawa), finished in 2003. The facade has a soft, wavy look.
best: Visit at dusk, when the lit facade glows through the glass.
booking: Viewing from the street is free. You do not need a ticket.

name: Ginza Six
why: Large shopping complex from 2017 designed by Yoshio Taniguchi. It has a 4,000 square meter rooftop garden and a Noh theater.
best: Go in the late afternoon and stay for dinner. The rooftop garden is pleasant at dusk.
booking: Entry is free. The Noh theater and some events need separate tickets.

name: Suntory Museum of Art (Tokyo Midtown)
yomi: サントリーびじゅつかん
why: Art museum on the third floor of Tokyo Midtown Galleria. Kengo Kuma designed the interior with wooden lattice screens.
best: Go on a Friday evening, when the museum stays open until 8 pm.
booking: Ticket prices change with each exhibition, so check the museum site. The museum closes on Tuesdays and between shows.

name: Ginza Sony Park
why: Open-plan art and culture space in Ginza. It fully opened on January 26, 2025, on the site of the old Sony Building.
architect: Yoshinobu Ashihara (original Sony Building), 1966; Sony design team led by Daisuke Nagano, 2025
best: Visit in the afternoon or early evening. The rooftop shows the Sukiyabashi crossing.
booking: Entry is free. Exhibits and events change often, so check the schedule.

name: Koishikawa Korakuen
yomi: こいしかわこうらくえん
why: Edo-era stroll garden started in 1629, with a pond, bridges, and maple trees. It sits beside Tokyo Dome.
best: Go in the morning. Fall color usually peaks in late November or early December.
booking: Entry costs 300 yen. The garden opens from 9 am to 5 pm, and you need no ticket in advance.

name: Hamarikyu Gardens
yomi: はまりきゅうおんしていえん
why: Tidal-pond garden at the edge of Tokyo Bay, with a teahouse on the water. It is a Special Place of Scenic Beauty.
best: Go in the afternoon and drink matcha at the teahouse. Fall color builds from late November.
booking: Entry costs 300 yen. Pay at the gate. The water bus from Asakusa also stops here.

name: Hoshinoya Tokyo
why: Tall ryokan-style hotel in Otemachi with a hot spring bath on the top floor. It opened in July 2016.
best: Soak in the rooftop bath in the evening, when the office towers glow.
booking: Reserve many months ahead on the Hoshino Resorts site. Rooms fill fast in the fall.

name: Thermae-Yu (Shinjuku)
why: Modern urban onsen complex in Kabukicho with baths and rock saunas. It stays open all day and all night.
best: Go in the evening after a long day of walking. The baths stay open through the night.
booking: You do not need a reservation. Entry costs about 2,900 yen, and the website sells discount tickets.

name: Japan National Stadium
yomi: こくりつきょうぎじょう
why: Kengo Kuma's Olympic stadium with timber eaves, opened in December 2019.
best: Walk around the outside in daylight to see the timber eaves.
booking: Viewing the outside is free. Inside access needs an event ticket, so check the stadium site.

name: 21_21 Design Sight
yomi: トゥーワントゥーワンデザインサイト
why: Tadao Ando's low design museum in the Tokyo Midtown garden, created with Issey Miyake. A folded steel roof covers the galleries.
best: Go in the afternoon, then walk through the Midtown garden.
booking: Pay at the door. The museum closes on Tuesdays and between exhibitions.

name: Rikugien
why: Stroll garden built between 1695 and 1702 for Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu. Its maples glow during the fall evening light-up.
best: Fall color usually peaks in late November. The evening light-up often runs from late November into early December.
booking: Entry costs 300 yen. Evening light-up tickets cost about 900 to 1,000 yen in advance online, and dates change each year.

name: Tokyo International Forum
yomi: とうきょうこくさいフォーラム
why: Rafael Viñoly's cultural complex from 1996, with a soaring glass atrium. The curved steel and glass hall draws architecture fans.
best: Walk through the atrium on a sunny afternoon, when light crosses the glass.
booking: The atrium is free to enter. Events inside need their own tickets.

name: Hakone Shrine
why: Cedar-shaded shrine on the shore of Lake Ashi. The red Peace Torii stands in the water in front of it.
best: Go at sunrise for calm light on the lake and the torii. Red maples line the approach in November.
booking: Entry is free. You do not need a ticket.

name: Hakone Open-Air Museum
yomi: ちょうこくのもりびじゅつかん
why: Outdoor sculpture park that opened in 1969. Its Picasso Pavilion holds about 300 works.
best: Go in the morning in early to mid November, when red leaves frame the sculptures.
booking: Buy tickets at the gate or online. The museum opens daily from 9 am to 5 pm.

name: Owakudani
why: Active volcanic valley with steam vents and a sulfur smell. Visitors eat black eggs boiled in the hot springs.
best: Go on a clear morning for views of Mount Fuji. Colors around the valley peak from late October to mid November.
booking: You do not need a ticket for the valley. The ropeway sells its own ticket, and volcanic gas can close the area.

name: Hakone-Yumoto Onsen
yomi: はこねゆもとおんせん
why: Hot spring town at the start of the Hakone Tozan line, with many onsen inns and shops near the station.
best: Arrive in the morning and stay a night. Fall color peaks in mid to late November, later than higher areas.
booking: Walking the town is free. Book onsen inns well ahead for November weekends.

name: Gora Kadan
why: Luxury ryokan in a former imperial villa, with gardens and open-air baths. It stands a few minutes from Gora Station.
architect: Amorph (Kiyoshi Takeyama and Kunio Ogitsu), 1989 renewal of a 1930 villa
best: Stay in early to mid November, when the maples in Gora are at their best.
booking: Book many months ahead on the official site. Dinner and breakfast come with the stay.

name: Hakone Venetian Glass Museum
kanji: 箱根ガラスの森美術館
yomi: はこねガラスのもりびじゅつかん
why: Museum of Venetian glass from the 15th to 18th centuries, with a garden of glass sculptures in Sengokuhara.
best: Visit on a clear afternoon, when sunlight makes the garden glass sparkle.
booking: Pay at the gate. The museum opens from 10 am to 5:30 pm, and adult entry costs about 1,800 yen.

name: POLA Museum of Art
why: Art museum in a protected forest, with a glass-walled main building. A short nature trail circles the grounds.
best: Walk the 670 meter nature trail first, then visit the galleries. Sengokuhara colors peak in early to mid November.
booking: Pay at the entrance. Prices change with each exhibition, so check the museum site.

name: Hakone Gora Park
yomi: はこねごうらこうえん
why: Japan's first French-style garden, opened in 1914, with a fountain, roses, and greenhouses on a slope above Gora.
best: Visit in the afternoon, when light warms the maples. Colors peak in early to mid November, so late November may be past peak.
booking: Entry costs about 550 yen. Pay at the gate. The last entry is at 4:30 pm.

name: Arakurayama Sengen Park (Chureito Pagoda)
yomi: あらくらやませんげんこうえん
why: Park with a red five-story pagoda that frames Mount Fuji. The pagoda dates from 1963, and 398 steps lead up to it.
best: Go at sunrise on a clear weekday. Fall color runs from late October through November.
booking: Entry is free and the site stays open all day. You do not need a ticket.

name: Oshino Hakkai
why: Eight clear spring-fed ponds in a village at the foot of Mount Fuji. The site is part of the Mount Fuji World Heritage Site.
best: Go early in the morning before the tour buses arrive. Mount Fuji shows best on clear days.
booking: Walking among the ponds is free. The Hannoki Bayashi Shiryokan museum costs 300 yen.

name: Kubota Itchiku Art Museum
yomi: くぼたいっちくびじゅつかん
why: Museum of Itchiku Kubota's dyed kimono art. It sits in a hillside garden with a Noh stage north of Lake Kawaguchi.
best: Visit in the morning, then walk to the nearby Momiji Corridor. November is the peak maple season.
booking: Pay at the entrance. Adult entry costs 1,300 yen, and the museum opens daily from April to November.

name: Hoshinoya Fuji
why: Glamping resort with 40 cabins above Lake Kawaguchi and views of Mount Fuji. It is a resort, not a ryokan, and opened in October 2015.
best: Stay one or two nights. Lake Kawaguchi colors peak in November, and clear days show Mount Fuji.
booking: Reserve many months ahead on the Hoshino Resorts site. Rooms fill fast for fall dates.

name: Kawaguchiko Momiji Corridor
yomi: かわぐちこもみじかいろう
why: Tunnel of red maples along the Nashi River on the north shore of Lake Kawaguchi. Trees glow at night during the fall festival.
best: Visit in November, when the peak usually runs from early to late November. Go after dusk for the light-up.
booking: Entry is free. The light-up runs from sunset to about 9 pm during the autumn leaves festival.

name: Kiyomizu-dera
why: A wooden stage juts out over the hillside and gives a wide view of the city.
best: Arrive when the gates open for fewer people. Late November brings strong maple color around the stage.
booking: Buy a ticket at the gate. No reservation is needed. The temple holds special evening openings on some dates, so check the schedule.

name: Fushimi Inari Taisha
yomi: ふしみいなりたいしゃ
why: Thousands of red torii gates climb Mount Inari. The paths stay open all day and all night.
best: Go at sunrise or after dark for fewer people. The upper trail shows some fall color in late November.
booking: Entry is free and the shrine is always open. No ticket or reservation is needed.

name: Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion)
why: A gold-leaf pavilion stands over a mirror pond. A fire destroyed the original in 1950. The temple rebuilt it in 1955.
best: Visit at 9:00 when the gate opens, or near closing, for softer light. Late November adds maple color around the pond.
booking: Buy a paper ticket at the gate. No reservation is needed.

name: Ginkaku-ji (Silver Pavilion)
why: A hillside Zen temple with a moss garden and a sand garden. The pavilion itself never received silver leaf.
best: Go in the morning for soft light on the moss. Maples around the pond turn red in late November.
booking: Buy a ticket at the gate. No reservation is needed.

name: Ryoan-ji
why: A famous dry rock garden with fifteen stones on raked white gravel. A pond garden with maples lies behind it.
best: Sit on the veranda when the temple opens, before the tour groups arrive. Maples around the pond color in late November.
booking: Buy a ticket at the gate. No reservation is needed.

name: Tenryu-ji
why: A Zen temple in Arashiyama with a pond garden from the 14th century. Muso Soseki designed the garden.
best: Arrive at 8:30 when the gate opens. Late November is the usual peak for fall color in Arashiyama.
booking: Buy a garden ticket at the gate. A separate ticket adds the main halls. No reservation is needed.

name: Arashiyama Bamboo Grove
why: A footpath winds between tall green bamboo stalks next to Tenryu-ji. The stalks sway and rustle in the wind.
best: Walk before 8:00 for the quietest hour. Fall color nearby peaks in late November.
booking: Entry is free and the path needs no ticket.

name: Tofuku-ji
why: A Zen temple famous for fall color. The covered Tsutenkyo bridge crosses a valley full of maples.
best: Colors usually peak in mid to late November. Arrive at 8:30 when the gate opens, because the bridge gets very crowded.
booking: Buy tickets at the gate. Fees are higher from mid-November in the fall color season. No reservation is needed.

name: Nanzen-ji
why: A large Zen complex with a brick aqueduct and a huge Sanmon gate. The grounds are free to walk.
best: Go in the morning, then walk to Eikan-do nearby. Maples around the aqueduct color in late November.
booking: The grounds are free. Buy separate tickets for the Hojo garden and the Sanmon gate. No reservation is needed.

name: Kyoto Imperial Palace
why: A former imperial residence, rebuilt in 1855, inside a large park. Visitors walk the grounds and see the outer halls.
best: Go on a dry morning. Ginkgo and maple color in the surrounding park peaks in late November.
booking: Entry is free and no reservation is needed. Use the Seishomon gate on the west side. The palace closes on Mondays.

name: Kyoto Station
why: Hiroshi Hara designed this huge glass and steel terminal, which opened in 1997. A sky path and a rooftop terrace give views over the city.
best: Visit at dusk for city lights from the rooftop. The building also works well on rainy days.
booking: Entry is free. The rooftop terrace and the sky path need no ticket.

name: Kyoto National Museum
yomi: きょうとこくりつはくぶつかん
why: A major museum for Buddhist art and national treasures. A brick hall from 1895 stands beside a modern wing by Yoshio Taniguchi.
best: Go on a weekday morning, then visit Sanjusangendo next door. The grounds look pleasant in fall.
booking: Buy a ticket at the door. Large special shows can have long lines, so check the official site. The museum closes on Mondays.

name: Nintendo Museum
yomi: にんてんどうミュージアム
why: A museum of Nintendo history inside a former factory in Uji, about 20 minutes from Kyoto Station. It opened in October 2024.
best: Choose a weekday slot if you can. Allow several hours for the exhibits and the play areas.
booking: Entry is by lottery on the official site. You need a free Nintendo Account, a credit card and ID. Entries open about three months ahead.

name: Tawaraya
why: A famous inn of about 300 years in central Kyoto. Guests stay in quiet rooms with garden views.
best: Plan for the evening, when the dinner and the courtyard gardens are at their best. Maples color in late November.
booking: Book by email in English, and write as early as you can. The inn replies with room details and rates.

name: Daitoku-ji
why: A large Zen complex with many sub-temples and dry gardens. It is quieter than the main temples in Higashiyama.
best: Go on a weekday morning. Maples in the sub-temple gardens color in late November.
booking: Entry to the grounds is free. Each open sub-temple sells its own ticket. Many sub-temples stay closed to visitors.

name: Kodai-ji
why: Nene, the widow of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, founded this temple in 1606. Its garden and bamboo grove glow under lights in the evening.
best: Visit in the evening if the autumn light-up runs during your trip. Maple color peaks in late November.
booking: Buy a ticket at the gate. The evening light-up runs only on set dates, so check the official dates before you go.

name: Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art
yomi: きょうとしきょうせらびじゅつかん
why: A 1933 museum in Okazaki with a Japanese-style roof on a Western plan. Jun Aoki and Tezzo Nishizawa renovated it, and it reopened in 2020.
architect: Maeda Kenjiro, 1933; Jun Aoki and Tezzo Nishizawa, 2020
best: Visit on a weekday morning for a quiet lobby and garden. Heian Shrine and Nanzen-ji are a short walk away.
booking: Special exhibitions need a ticket. Check the official site for dates and online booking.

name: Hiiragiya
why: A ryokan open since 1818, close to Tawaraya on the same street. It has a historic main building and a newer wing from 2006.
best: Stay one night for the kaiseki dinner and the tofu breakfast. Garden maples glow in late November.
booking: Book on the official site, by email or by phone. Reserve as early as you can for November.

name: Eikan-do (Zenrin-ji)
yomi: えいかんどうぜんりんじ
why: A temple famous for fall color, with a pond garden and many maple trees. Its Buddha statue looks back over its shoulder.
best: Visit at opening time or at night in the late November peak. The evening light-up usually runs from early November to early December.
booking: Buy a ticket at the gate. Fall season fees are higher, and the evening light-up has its own ticket. Check the official site for 2027 dates.

name: Byodo-in
why: The Phoenix Hall of 1053 stands on a pond and appears on the ten-yen coin. It is a UNESCO World Heritage building in Uji.
best: Visit on a weekday at opening time. Maples around the pond color in late November and early December.
booking: Buy a garden ticket at the gate. Pay a little more for the Phoenix Hall interior tour, sold in the garden. Groups enter every 20 minutes.

name: Kyoto Railway Museum
yomi: きょうとてつどうはくぶつかん
why: A large railway museum with real trains from steam locomotives to shinkansen cars. A fan-shaped roundhouse holds many steam locomotives.
best: Go on a weekday morning, since weekends and school holidays are busy. The museum also suits a rainy day.
booking: Buy advance tickets online for smooth entry. The museum closes on Wednesdays.

name: Todai-ji
why: The Great Buddha Hall is one of the largest wooden buildings in the world. It houses a bronze Buddha about 15 meters tall.
best: Arrive at 8:00 when the hall opens for fewer people. Maples near Kagami-ike pond turn red in late November.
booking: Buy a ticket at the gate and pay in cash. No reservation is needed.

name: Kasuga Taisha
why: A hill shrine known for thousands of lanterns along a forest path. Deer walk freely on the approach.
best: Go in the morning for a quiet forest walk. Maples along the approach color in late November.
booking: The outer grounds are free. Buy a ticket at the gate for the inner shrine area. No reservation is needed.

name: Kofuku-ji
why: A major temple with a five-story pagoda from 1426. It also holds the Central Golden Hall, rebuilt in 2018.
best: Visit in the late afternoon for soft light on the pagoda above Sarusawa Pond. Maples color in late November.
booking: The grounds are free. Buy separate tickets for the Central Golden Hall, the Eastern Golden Hall and the National Treasure Museum.

name: Nara Park
why: A large park with more than a thousand free-roaming deer. It links Todai-ji, Kasuga Taisha and the museums.
best: Walk in the early morning for calm deer and soft light. Park maples peak in late November.
booking: Entry is free. Buy deer crackers only from the official stalls. No reservation is needed.

name: Isui-en
why: A garden in two parts, from the Edo and Meiji periods. It borrows Mount Wakakusa and the Nandaimon gate of Todai-ji as scenery.
best: Visit in the morning on a day without rain. The maples turn red in late November.
booking: Buy a ticket at the gate. The garden closes on Tuesdays and during short maintenance periods.

name: Nara National Museum
yomi: ならこくりつはくぶつかん
why: A museum of Buddhist art in a fine 1894 hall. A yearly autumn show displays treasures from the Shosoin storehouse.
best: The Shosoin show usually runs from late October to mid-November, so check the 2027 dates before you plan the day.
booking: Buy tickets at the door. The autumn show can have long lines, so check the official site for timed tickets.

name: Nara Hotel
why: A classic hotel that opened in 1909 near Nara Park. Tatsuno Kingo designed the main building with a Japanese-style roof.
best: Stay for dinner and the quiet evening after day visitors leave. Park maples color in late November.
booking: Book rooms early on the official site for November. Guests who do not stay can eat at the hotel restaurants.

name: Yoshiki-en
why: A small garden with a pond garden, a moss garden and a tea flower garden. Mount Wakakusa rises behind it.
best: Visit in the morning in late November, when maples glow against the green moss.
booking: Entry is free. Only the tea room needs a reservation. The garden closes from February 24 to 28.

name: Osaka Castle
why: A castle with a main tower rebuilt in concrete in 1931. It stands inside a large park with stone walls and moats.
best: Visit in the morning, then walk the moat paths. Ginkgo and maple color in the park peaks from late November.
booking: Buy a tower ticket at the site or online to skip the line. The park is free to enter.

name: Sumiyoshi Taisha
why: One of the oldest shrines in Japan, with a steep arched bridge. Its main halls follow the rare Sumiyoshi style.
best: Go on a weekday morning for quiet paths. Fall color is light here, so plan the visit for the architecture.
booking: Entry is free. No ticket or reservation is needed.

name: Shitennoji
why: Osaka's oldest temple, founded in 593. Its gate, pagoda and halls stand in a straight line from south to north, in an ancient temple layout.
best: Go in the morning for a calm walk through the inner precinct. Evening light on the pagoda also looks good.
booking: The outer grounds are free. Buy a ticket at the gate for the inner precinct and the garden.

name: Umeda Sky Building
why: Two towers join near the top at a floating-garden observatory. Hiroshi Hara designed the building, and it opened in 1993.
best: Go at sunset to watch the city change from day to night. The open-air deck stays open until 22:30.
booking: Buy tickets at the site or online. Online tickets let you skip the ticket line. The deck may close in heavy rain.

name: Nakanoshima Museum of Art
yomi: おおさかなかのしまびじゅつかん
why: A modern art museum in a black box-shaped building on the Nakanoshima river island. It opened in 2022 and shows modern art and design.
best: Go in the afternoon and stay for the evening views of the river.
booking: Buy exhibition tickets at the desk or on the official site. The museum closes on Mondays.

name: Church of the Light
why: Tadao Ando's small concrete chapel has a cross cut into the wall behind the altar. It stands in a quiet neighborhood of Ibaraki city.
best: Morning light gives the strongest glow through the cross opening.
booking: Visitor tours have been suspended since 2024. Check the church website and reserve in advance before you plan the trip.

name: Chikatsu-Asuka Historical Museum
yomi: ちかつあすかはくぶつかん
why: Tadao Ando's museum stands in the hills of Kanan, next to ancient burial mounds. A stepped concrete roof doubles as an outdoor stair.
best: Visit on a dry weekday. The hills around the museum show fall color in late November.
booking: Buy a ticket at the door. The museum closes on Mondays. Its exhibition rooms were closed for renovation until March 2026, so confirm they are open.

name: Tower of the Sun (Expo '70)
why: Taro Okamoto's 70-meter sculpture from Expo '70 stands in a large park. Visitors can now enter and see the Tree of Life inside.
best: Go in the morning on a clear day. Trees in the Japanese garden of the park may show color in late November.
booking: Reserve an entry time on the official website, because reserved visitors enter first. The park charges a separate fee.
